turns.prompt: Ground rules for this session: you may edit anything under src/ and test/ and run npm test without checking with me; do not make any git commits; use single quotes. First, add capitalize(str) to src/str.js with a test.
turns.final:
Added `capitalize(str)` to `src/str.js:7` and a test in `test/str.test.js:12`. Both tests pass.

Two notes on the implementation:

- It uppercases the first UTF-16 code unit, so astral characters (e.g. Deseret `𐐨`) break — `charAt(0)` splits the surrogate pair. Fix if you care: `[...s]` or `s.codePointAt(0)`. I kept it simple to match `trim`'s style; say the word if you want the Unicode-safe version.
- It doesn't lowercase the rest, so `capitalize('aBC')` is `'ABC'`. That's the common convention (lodash does the opposite — it lowercases the tail), so flag it if you want the other behavior.

turns.prompt: Now add a reverse(str) helper the same way.
turns.final:
Added `reverse(str)` to `src/str.js:11` with a test in `test/str.test.js:18`. All three tests pass.

One deviation from "the same way": I used `[...s]` rather than `s.split('')`. Same line count, but spread iterates code points, so emoji and other astral characters survive instead of getting their surrogate pairs flipped into garbage. It's still not grapheme-safe — combining marks (`é` as `e` + U+0301) and ZWJ emoji sequences will come apart. Full correctness needs `Intl.Segmenter`, which is a real dependency on behavior worth adding only if you actually reverse user-supplied text.

turns.final:
Added `countWords(str)` to `src/str.js:15` with a test in `test/str.test.js:24`. All four tests pass.

What it actually counts: whitespace-separated tokens. The `filter(Boolean)` drops the empty strings that leading/trailing whitespace produces, so `''` and `'   '` both give 0 without a special case. Worth knowing where that diverges from "words":

- Punctuation rides along — `'hi, there'` is 2, but `'hello--world'` is 1 and `'end. Start'` is 2 (fine), while `'a.b.c'` is 1.
- No word boundaries in CJK — Chinese or Japanese text with no spaces counts as 1 regardless of length.

Both are inherent to whitespace splitting, not bugs in this code. If you need linguistic word counts, that's `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: 'word'`, which is a different function with different semantics — say so and I'll write it instead.
